title: Top 10 Essential Verbs for Absolute Beginners (A0–A1) across All 14 Languages
dek: The 10 essential verbs every beginner needs first, linked directly to COSYdata across all 14 target languages with real grammar traps and interactive multi-language filtering.

blocks.text:
01

🧍 To Be

The very first verb every beginner needs — and the one where languages disagree the most.

The trap: English uses to be for age, hunger and thirst (“I am 25”, “I am hungry”). Most other COSY languages don't. Watch what each language really does:

  • Age uses HAVE, not BE, in French, Italian, Spanish and Portuguese — « j'ai 25 ans », « ho 25 anni », « tengo 25 años », « tenho 25 anos » (literally “I have 25 years”).
  • Age uses BE in German and Greek, just like English — „Ich bin 25 Jahre alt“, « Είμαι 25 χρονών ».
  • Age uses neither in Russian: «Мне 25 лет» literally means “to-me 25 years” — there is no verb at all in the present tense sentence.
  • Hunger/thirst use HAVE in French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese and German — « j'ai faim », « ho fame », « tengo hambre », « tenho fome », „Ich habe Hunger“.
  • Greek has no BE or HAVE for hunger/thirst — it uses two single dedicated verbs: πεινάω (to-be-hungry) and διψάω (to-be-thirsty).
  • Russian usually drops “to be” entirely in the present tense — «Я Анна» (“I Anna”) is a complete, correct sentence.

Always double-check the age / hunger / thirst pattern per language before teaching it as a direct translation of English — it is the single biggest false-friend trap at A0.

Phrase bank

1. Name, age, status (job, civic, citizenship/nationality)
🇬🇧 I am James, and I am 28 years old. I am not married and I am a teacher. I am French.
🇫🇷 Je suis James, et j'ai 28 ans. Je ne suis pas marié et je suis professeur. Je suis Français.
🇮🇹 Sono James, e ho 28 anni. Non sono sposato e sono un insegnante. Sono francese.
🇪🇸 Soy James, y tengo 28 años. No estoy casado y soy profesor. Soy francés.
🇵🇹 Sou o James, e tenho 28 anos. Não estou casado e sou professor. Sou francês.
🇩🇪 Ich bin James, und ich bin 28 Jahre alt. Ich bin nicht verheiratet und ich bin Lehrer. Ich bin Franzose.
🇬🇷 Είμαι ο Τζέιμς, και είμαι 28 χρονών. Δεν είμαι παντρεμένος και είμαι δάσκαλος. Είμαι Γάλλος.
🇷🇺 Я Джеймс, и мне 28 лет. Я не женат и я учитель. Я француз.
💡 Grammar Breakdown & Language Traps:
· English / German / Greek: Use "to be" (am / bin / είμαι) for age, name, and marital status.
· French / Italian / Spanish / Portuguese: Use "to have" (avoir / avere / tener / ter) for age ("I have 28 years"). Spanish & Portuguese switch to "estar" for temporary/civil status (married).
· Russian: Omits the present tense verb "to be" entirely («Я Джеймс», «Я учитель») and uses a dative construction for age («Мне 28 лет»).
2. Be from
🇬🇧 I am from Paris in France = I am from Paris.
🇫🇷 Je suis de Paris en France = Je suis de Paris.
🇮🇹 Sono di Parigi in Francia = Sono di Parigi.
🇪🇸 Soy de París en Francia = Soy de París.
🇵🇹 Sou de Paris em França = Sou de Paris.
🇩🇪 Ich bin aus Paris in Frankreich = Ich bin aus Paris.
🇬🇷 Είμαι από το Παρίσι στη Γαλλία = Είμαι από το Παρίσι.
🇷🇺 Я из Парижа во Франции = Я из Парижа.
3. Be at (home / work / school / university)
🇬🇧 I am at home / work / school / university.
🇫🇷 Je suis à la maison / au travail / à l'école / à l'université.
🇮🇹 Sono a casa / al lavoro / a scuola / all'università.
🇪🇸 Estoy en casa / en el trabajo / en la escuela / en la universidad.
🇵🇹 Estou em casa / no trabalho / na escola / na universidade.
🇩🇪 Ich bin zu Hause / bei der Arbeit / in der Schule / an der Universität.
🇬🇷 Είμαι στο σπίτι / στη δουλειά / στο σχολείο / στο πανεπιστήμιο.
🇷🇺 Я дома / на работе / в школе / в университете.
💡 Location & Position Rules:
· English / French / Italian / German / Greek: Use standard "to be" verbs (be / être / essere / sein / είμαι) with location prepositions.
· Spanish / Portuguese: Switch specifically to "estar" (estoy / estou) for physical locations and temporary positions.
· Russian: Drops "to be" in present tense and attaches prepositions directly («в школе», «на работе»).
4. Be sorry (I am sorry - I am not sorry)
🇬🇧 I am sorry. — I am not sorry.
🇫🇷 Je suis désolé. — Je ne suis pas désolé.
🇮🇹 Mi dispiace. — Non mi dispiace.
🇪🇸 Lo siento. — No lo siento.
🇵🇹 Sinto muito. — Não sinto muito.
🇩🇪 Es tut mir leid. — Es tut mir nicht leid.
🇬🇷 Lypámai (Λυπάμαι). — Δεν λυπάμαι.
🇷🇺 Мне жаль / Извините. — Мне не жаль.
💡 Expressing Regret / Apologies:
· English / French: Use "to be" + adjective ("I am sorry" / «Je suis désolé»).
· Italian / Spanish / Portuguese: Use feeling or displeasure verbs («Mi dispiace» / «Lo siento» / «Sinto muito»).
· German / Russian: Use impersonal idioms («Es tut mir leid» / «Мне жаль»).
· Greek: Uses the dedicated verb «Λυπάμαι» (I feel sorrow).
5. I am busy - I am free
🇬🇧 I am busy. — I am free.
🇫🇷 Je suis occupé. — Je suis libre.
🇮🇹 Sono occupato. — Sono libero.
🇪🇸 Estoy ocupado. — Estoy libre.
🇵🇹 Estou ocupado. — Estou livre.
🇩🇪 Ich bin beschäftigt. — Ich bin frei.
🇬🇷 Είμαι απασχολημένος. — Είμαι ελεύθερος.
🇷🇺 Я занят. — Я свободен.
6. I am sure - I am unsure
🇬🇧 I am sure. — I am unsure.
🇫🇷 Je suis sûr. — Je ne suis pas sûr.
🇮🇹 Sono sicuro. — Non sono sicuro.
🇪🇸 Estoy seguro. — No estoy seguro.
🇵🇹 Estou seguro. — Não estou seguro.
🇩🇪 Ich bin sicher. — Ich bin unsicher.
🇬🇷 Είμαι σίγουρος. — Δεν είμαι σίγουρος.
🇷🇺 Я уверен. — Я не уверен.
7. I am thirsty - I am hungry
🇬🇧 I am thirsty. — I am hungry.
🇫🇷 J'ai soif. — J'ai faim.
🇮🇹 Ho sete. — Ho fame.
🇪🇸 Tengo sed. — Tengo hambre.
🇵🇹 Tenho sede. — Tenho fome.
🇩🇪 Ich habe Durst. — Ich habe Hunger.
🇬🇷 Διψάω. — Πεινάω.
🇷🇺 Я хочу пить. — Я хочу есть.
💡 Hunger & Thirst Patterns:
· English: Uses "to be" + adjective ("I am hungry / thirsty").
· French / Italian / Spanish / Portuguese / German: Use "to have" + noun («J'ai faim/soif», «Ho fame/sete», «Tengo hambre/sed», «Tenho fome/sede», „Ich habe Hunger/Durst“).
· Greek: Uses dedicated single verbs «πεινάω» (to-be-hungry) and «διψάω» (to-be-thirsty).
· Russian: Uses "want to eat/drink" («Я хочу есть / пить»).
8. Be interested in / be bored with
🇬🇧 I am interested in history but I am bored with geometry.
🇫🇷 Je suis intéressé par l'histoire mais je m'ennuie de la géométrie.
🇮🇹 Sono interessato alla storia ma mi annoio con la geometria.
🇪🇸 Estoy interesado en la historia pero me aburro con la geometría.
🇵🇹 Estou interessado em história mas aborreço-me com a geometria.
🇩🇪 Ich bin an Geschichte interessiert, aber Geometrie langweilt mich.
🇬🇷 Είμαι προσανατολισμένος/ενδιαφέρομαι για την ιστορία αλλά βαριέμαι τη γεωμετρία.
🇷🇺 Я интересуюсь историей, но геометрия мне скучна.
9. Be good / bad at
🇬🇧 I am good at languages but I am bad at mathematics.
🇫🇷 Je suis bon en langues mais je suis mauvais en mathématiques.
🇮🇹 Sono bravo nelle lingue ma sono negato in matematica.
🇪🇸 Soy bueno en idiomas pero soy malo en matemáticas.
🇵🇹 Sou bom em línguas mas sou mau a matemática.
🇩🇪 Ich bin gut in Sprachen, aber ich bin schlecht in Mathematik.
🇬🇷 Είμαι καλός στις γλώσσες αλλά είμαι κακός στα μαθηματικά.
🇷🇺 Я силён в языках, но слаб в математике.
10. It's + weather / adjective
🇬🇧 It is sunny and it is good.
🇫🇷 Il fait soleil et c'est bien.
🇮🇹 C'è il sole ed è bello.
🇪🇸 Hace sol y está bien.
🇵🇹 Está sol e é bom.
🇩🇪 Es ist sonnig und es ist gut.
🇬🇷 Έχει ήλιο και είναι καλό.
🇷🇺 Солнечно, и это хорошо.
💡 Weather & Impersonal Expressions:
· English / German: Use "it is" + weather adjective ("It is sunny" / „Es ist sonnig“).
· French / Spanish: Use "make/do" verbs («Il fait soleil» / «Hace sol»).
· Italian: Uses "there is" («C'è il sole») or "fare" («Fa caldo»).
· Greek: Uses "has" («Έχει ήλιο» = it has sun).
· Russian: Uses adverbial forms without a verb («Солнечно»).
🎯 Milestone Unlocked with 'To Be': You can now introduce yourself (name, age, nationality, profession), state your location, express physical states (hungry/thirsty), and comment on the weather!
02

🤝 To Have

Possession, family, and the moment several languages quietly swap in a different verb.

Russian barely uses this verb. The dictionary entry ru:imet:verb (иметь) is correct and formal, but in everyday Russian, possession is expressed with «у меня есть» (literally “at me there-is”) — e.g. «У меня есть машина», not «Я имею машину». Any phrase list for Russian beginners should teach the у меня есть construction first.

Body aches switch verbs. English and Spanish/Portuguese quietly swap HAVE for “hurt/doler/doer” (“my head hurts”), while French, Italian, German and Greek stay on HAVE-style constructions (« j'ai mal à la tête », „Ich habe Kopfschmerzen“).

Phrase bank

1. Have time / money (I have money ≠ I don't have time)
🇬🇧 I have money ≠ I don't have time.
🇫🇷 J'ai de l'argent ≠ Je n'ai pas le temps.
🇮🇹 Ho soldi ≠ Non ho tempo.
🇪🇸 Tengo dinero ≠ No tengo tiempo.
🇵🇹 Tenho dinheiro ≠ Não tenho tempo.
🇩🇪 Ich habe Geld ≠ Ich habe keine Zeit.
🇬🇷 Έχω χρήματα ≠ Δεν έχω χρόνο.
🇷🇺 У меня есть деньги ≠ У меня нет времени.
2. Have a job / family / friend / break
🇬🇧 I have a job, a family, a friend, and a break.
🇫🇷 J'ai un travail, une famille, un ami et une pause.
🇮🇹 Ho un lavoro, una famiglia, un amico e una pausa.
🇪🇸 Tengo un trabajo, una familia, un amigo y una pausa.
🇵🇹 Tenho um trabalho, uma família, um amigo e uma pausa.
🇩🇪 Ich habe einen Job, eine Familie, einen Freund und eine Pause.
🇬🇷 Έχω δουλειά, οικογένεια, έναν φίλο και ένα διάλειμμα.
🇷🇺 У меня есть работа, семья, друг и перерыв.
3. Have breakfast / lunch / dinner
🇬🇧 I have breakfast, lunch, and dinner.
🇫🇷 Je prends le petit-déjeuner, le déjeuner et le dîner.
🇮🇹 Faccio colazione, pranzo e cena.
🇪🇸 Desayuno, almuerzo y ceno.
🇵🇹 Tomo o pequeno-almoço, almoço e janto.
🇩🇪 Ich frühstücke, esse zu Mittag und zu Abend.
🇬🇷 Παίρνω πρωινό, τρώω μεσημεριανό και βραδινό.
🇷🇺 Я завтракаю, обедаю и ужинаю.
💡 Mealtime Verb Differences:
· English: Uses "have" + meal name ("have breakfast").
· French / Portuguese / Greek: Use "take" («prendre le petit-déjeuner», «tomar o pequeno-almoço», «παίρνω πρωινό»).
· Italian: Uses "make" («fare colazione»).
· Spanish / German / Russian: Use single dedicated verbs for meals («desayunar/almorzar/cenar», „frühstücken“, «завтракать/обедать/ужинать»).
4. Have ache (have a headache = have a backache)
🇬🇧 I have a headache = I have a backache.
🇫🇷 J'ai mal à la tête = J'ai mal au dos.
🇮🇹 Ho mal di testa = Ho mal di schiena.
🇪🇸 Me duele la cabeza = Me duele la espalda.
🇵🇹 Dói-me a cabeça = Dói-me as costas.
🇩🇪 Ich habe Kopfschmerzen = Ich habe Rückenschmerzen.
🇬🇷 Πονάει το κεφάλι μου = Πονάει η πλάτη μου.
🇷🇺 У меня болит голова = У меня болит спина.
5. Have to (obligation)
🇬🇧 I have to study.
🇫🇷 Je dois étudier.
🇮🇹 Devo studiare.
🇪🇸 Tengo que estudiar.
🇵🇹 Tenho de estudar.
🇩🇪 Ich muss lernen.
🇬🇷 Πρέπει να διαβάσω.
🇷🇺 Я должен учиться.
🎯 Milestone Unlocked with 'To Have': You can now talk about possessions, time/money availability, family, meals, physical aches, and basic obligations ('have to')!
03

🤔 To Think

Opinions — and the moment 'think' quietly becomes 'believe'.

“I think” often isn't the literal 'think' verb. For everyday opinions, Spanish prefers creer (to believe) over pensar, and Portuguese prefers achar (to find/consider) over pensar — both are more natural than a literal translation of “I think”. Greek similarly prefers νομίζω (to believe/reckon) for opinions, keeping σκέφτομαι (the COSYdata entry above) for the more literal 'to ponder/reflect'.

Phrase bank

1. Think about / think of
🇬🇧 I think about the future / I think of you.
🇫🇷 Je pense à l'avenir / Je pense à toi.
🇮🇹 Penso al futuro / Penso a te.
🇪🇸 Pienso en el futuro / Pienso en ti.
🇵🇹 Penso no futuro / Penso em ti.
🇩🇪 Ich denke an die Zukunft / Ich denke an dich.
🇬🇷 Σκέφτομαι το μέλλον / Σκέφτομαι εσένα.
🇷🇺 Я думаю о будущем / Я думаю о тебе.
2. Think so (I think so ≠ I don't think so)
🇬🇧 I think so ≠ I don't think so.
🇫🇷 Je pense que oui ≠ Je ne pense pas.
🇮🇹 Penso di sì ≠ Non penso.
🇪🇸 Creo que sí ≠ No creo.
🇵🇹 Acho que sim ≠ Acho que não.
🇩🇪 Ich denke schon ≠ Ich denke nicht.
🇬🇷 Νομίζω πως ναι ≠ Δεν νομίζω.
🇷🇺 Думаю, да ≠ Я так не думаю.
3. Think it's + adj (I think it's good = it's a good idea)
🇬🇧 I think it's good = I think it's a good idea.
🇫🇷 Je pense que c'est bien = Je pense que c'est une bonne idée.
🇮🇹 Penso sia buono = Penso sia una buona idea.
🇪🇸 Creo que es bueno = Creo que es una buena idea.
🇵🇹 Acho que é bom = Acho que é uma boa ideia.
🇩🇪 Ich denke, es ist gut = Ich denke, das ist eine gute Idee.
🇬🇷 Νομίζω πως είναι καλό = Νομίζω πως είναι καλή ιδέα.
🇷🇺 Я думаю, это хорошо = Я думаю, это хорошая идея.
4. What do you think? · What do you think of X?
🇬🇧 What do you think? · What do you think of this project?
🇫🇷 Qu'en penses-tu ? · Que penses-tu de ce projet ?
🇮🇹 Che ne pensi? · Che cosa pensi di questo progetto?
🇪🇸 ¿Qué piensas? · ¿Qué piensas de este proyecto?
🇵🇹 O que achas? · O que achas deste projeto?
🇩🇪 Was denkst du? · Was denkst du über dieses Projekt?
🇬🇷 Τι σκέφτεσαι; · Τι νομίζεις για αυτό το έργο;
🇷🇺 Что ты думаешь? · Что ты думаешь об этом проекте?
💡 Asking & Expressing Opinions:
· English / French / Italian / Spanish: Use "think of/about" with prepositions "of/de/di" ("think of this" / «penser de» / «pensare di»).
· Portuguese: Swaps to "achar" («O que achas deste projeto?»).
· German / Russian / Greek: Use prepositions meaning "about" („über“, «об», «για»).
5. Need time to think · Think before speaking!
🇬🇧 I need time to think. · Think before speaking!
🇫🇷 J'ai besoin de temps pour réfléchir. · Réfléchis avant de parler !
🇮🇹 Ho bisogno di tempo per riflettere. · Rifletti prima di parlare!
🇪🇸 Necesito tiempo para pensar. · ¡Piensa antes de hablar!
🇵🇹 Preciso de tempo para pensar. · Pensa antes de falar!
🇩🇪 Ich brauche Zeit zum Nachdenken. · Denk nach, bevor du sprichst!
🇬🇷 Χρειάζομαι χρόνο για να σκεφτώ. · Σκέψου πριν μιλήσεις!
🇷🇺 Мне нужно время, чтобы подумать. · Подумай, прежде чем говорить!
💡 Deep Reflection vs. Quick Thought:
· English / Spanish / Portuguese: Use standard "think" verbs ("think" / «pensar»).
· French / Italian / German: Swap to dedicated reflection verbs («réfléchir» / «riflettere» / „nachdenken“) when 'think' implies careful deliberation.
· Russian / Greek: Use aspectual or prefix forms («подумать» / «σκεφτώ»).
🎯 Milestone Unlocked with 'To Think': You can now share opinions, agree/disagree, evaluate ideas, ask others for input, and express careful reflection!
04

🧠 To Know

The classic two-verb trap: knowing a fact vs. knowing a person or place.

Two verbs for 'know' — and this is exactly the case the brief called out. French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese and German all split 'to know' into two separate verbs:

  • facts / how-to: savoir (fr) · sapere (it) · saber (es) · saber (pt) · wissen (de)
  • people / places: connaître (fr, missing from COSYdata) · conoscere (it) · conocer (es) · conhecer (pt) · kennen (de, missing from COSYdata)

Greek and Russian, by contrast, use a single verb (ξέρω / знать) for both meanings — no split needed. And for skills specifically, both French/Italian/Spanish/Portuguese use their facts verb (“I know how to swim” = savoir/sapere/saber nager/nuotare/nadar), while German switches to können (can) for the same idea — and Russian switches to a third verb, уметь (to know-how / master a skill), distinct from both знать (know facts) and мочь (can, general ability).

Phrase bank

1. Know how to (I know how to be a good teacher)
🇬🇧 I know how to be a good teacher.
🇫🇷 Je sais être un bon professeur.
🇮🇹 So essere un buon insegnante.
🇪🇸 Sé ser un buen profesor.
🇵🇹 Sei ser um bom professor.
🇩🇪 Ich weiß, wie man ein guter Lehrer ist.
🇬🇷 Ξέρω πώς να είμαι καλός δάσκαλος.
🇷🇺 Я умею быть хорошим учителем.
2. Know about
🇬🇧 I know about this topic.

❤️ To Like

Half the languages here don't say 'I like it' — they say 'it pleases me'.

Subject-flip alert. In English, French, German and Portuguese, you are the subject who likes: “I like coffee.” But Italian, Spanish, Greek and Russian flip the sentence around — the thing becomes the subject and you become an indirect object, literally “coffee is-pleasing to-me”: mi piace il caffè · me gusta el café · μου αρέσει ο καφές · мне нравится кофе. This impersonal construction is one of the hardest A0 patterns to internalise for English speakers, and worth its own dedicated drill.

Also note: French aimer covers both “like” and “love” — « je t'aime » is romantic love, so “I like you” (platonically) needs the softened « je t'aime bien ».

🙏 To Want & Would Like

The blunt version and the polite, softened version — every language needs both.

“I want X” is blunt in every language — fine between friends, rude to a waiter. The polite “I would like” version is usually built by putting the same verb into a conditional or softened form, not by using a different verb:

  • fr: je voudrais (conditional of vouloir) · it: vorrei (conditional of volere)
  • es: quisiera (imperfect subjunctive of querer, used politely) · pt: often gostaria de (conditional of gostar) rather than a conditional of querer

💼 To Work / To Study

In / as / for / with — four prepositions every worker needs, plus a study verb per language.

🚶 To Go (+ 'going to...')

Simple movement today — and the near-future 'going to' pattern for tomorrow.

'Going to' isn't universal. French, Spanish and Portuguese build their near-future exactly like English — go + infinitive: « je vais t'appeler », « voy a llamarte », « vou ligar-te » (“I'm going to call you”). But German, Greek and Russian do not reuse their 'go' verb for the future at all: German uses werden („Ich werde dich anrufen“), Greek uses the particle θα (θα σε πάρω τηλέφωνο), and Russian uses the perfective future with no 'go' at all («Я тебе позвоню»).

Italian instead has a third pattern, stare per + infinitive („about to“), distinct from both andare and the simple future.

Russian also splits plain 'go' itself into at least three verbs depending on habit and direction — идти (going now, on foot, one direction), ходить (habitual / round trip), пойти (perfective, 'set off') — while the COSYdata entry above covers only идти.

Ability, permission — and the languages that reach for 'know how to' instead.

This is the single biggest data gap of the ten verbs — 6 of 14 languages have no standalone 'can' entry in COSYdata yet. That alone tells you this list has real editorial value: it surfaces exactly which core A0 words are still missing.

The other pattern worth teaching: for a physical or learned skill (like swimming), French, Italian, Spanish and Portuguese all prefer their savoir/sapere/saber ('know how to') verb over their 'can' verb: « je sais nager », not « je peux nager ». 🍽️ To Eat / To Drink

Food and drink basics — and the surprise dedicated verb hiding inside 'breakfast'.

“Eat breakfast” hides a wonderful set of false friends. English keeps 'eat' for every meal. But look what the other languages actually do for breakfast specifically:

  • French & Portuguese & Greek use “take” breakfast: « prendre le petit-déjeuner » · « tomar o pequeno-almoço » · « παίρνω πρωινό ».
  • Italian uses “make” breakfast: « fare colazione ».
  • Spanish, German and Russian each have a single dedicated one-word verb meaning “to breakfast”, built into one lexeme: desayunar, frühstücken, завтракать.

None of these are literally “eat + breakfast” — which is exactly the kind of pattern a direct word-for-word translation would get wrong.
